body: Thank you for sharing this software!!!!

> Closes #6.
> 
> New optional layer showing nodes that opted in to Meshtastic's own public Map Reporting feature — the network's built-in "publish yourself to a public map" mechanism, over MQTT.
> 
> **Server**: `meshtasticProxy` (`vite.config.js`) keeps one persistent MQTT connection to `mqtt.meshtastic.org` (the project's own public broker, published read-only credentials), subscribed only to `msh/+/2/map/#`. It decodes exclusively unencrypted MapReport packets (portnum 73) via the official `@meshtastic/protobufs` definitions and never inspects or attempts to decrypt anything else on the wire — encrypted channel packets are dropped without being touched. An in-memory cache (capped 8000 nodes, swept every 15 min, 24h eviction, true LRU) is served as plain JSON from `/api/meshtastic/nodes`; validated live against the real broker end-to-end.
> 
> **Client**: `src/data/meshtasticNodes.js` polls that snapshot like any other layer. A node's `position_precision` (bits retained) is honored rather than flattened into a false-precision pin — meaningful uncertainty renders as a translucent circle, a high-precision report as a plain point. Per-node LIVE/STALE opacity independent of overall layer status.
> 
> `src/data/meshtasticMapReport.js` holds the pure helpers (id formatting, uncertainty radius, freshness bucketing) shared by server and client; `src/data/meshtasticDecode.js` isolates the protobuf-dependent decode so it never reaches the browser bundle (confirmed via a production build). Registered in `main.js` + `layerState.js`, voice/text aliases, attribution in `dataCredits.js` and `DATA_SOURCES.md`.
> 
> Includes a follow-up commit fixing two bugs a code-review pass found:
> - `update()` could resolve to `false` on a transient fetch failure, which `manager.js`'s enable-lifecycle treats as a fatal enable failure and bounces the layer's toggle back off instead of leaving it enabled to report the failure via `getStats()`.
> - The node-cache cap silently dropped brand-new nodes once full instead of evicting the oldest-seen one — fixed to true LRU.
> 
> 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

We health-poll all three of the camera catalogs you're using. Right now 252 of the 1,005 cameras in the City of Austin catalog are flagged as contradicted: feed URL not serving an image, one shared "camera unavailable" card sitting behind many different ids, or coordinates that don't match where the camera actually is. Caltrans is nearly clean (9 of 3,476) and TfL is clean (0 of 882). Austin is the one that bites, and it bites hardest on click-to-track handoff, since "nearest camera" and "nearest camera that's actually sending a picture" are different cameras about a quarter of the time.

One call to see it:

```
curl "https://datumfeed.com/api/cameras?city=austin&verificationStatus=contradicted&limit=5"
```

Each row carries the rule that caught it. If it's useful, `?minTrust=70` on the catalog fetch drops them before they reach the globe, no key needed to try it.

Same API also covers WSDOT, Ontario 511 and Ottawa, which is another ~3,600 cameras in places the current three don't reach, in the same schema.

Either way, nice work. The handoff feature is the best thing in it.

Two of those are fair and one isn't.

Fair: `browserModuleBoundary.test.mjs` is a textual scan by design — it guards the boundary (no `node:*` specifier in a browser-built module), not the loading. And the repo runs no CI, so there are no check results to show on any PR here.

**The Node path is covered**, just not by the file added here. Two test files already exercise these loaders, and this PR deletes the `fs` branch they used to take — `naturalEarthRegions.test.mjs` (`findNaturalRegion`, `lookupNaturalRegionOutline`, `listRegions` → `loadPackFile`) and `neighborhoodPolygons.test.mjs` (`lookupNeighborhoodRing` → `cityLoader`). On this branch, with `grep -c "node:fs"` returning 0 in both modules:

```
$ node --test src/data/naturalEarthRegions.test.mjs src/data/neighborhoodPolygons.test.mjs
# tests 20
# pass 20
# fail 0
```

With the fallback gone those 20 assertions can only pass through the import attribute.

**The browser build — I built both branches to check.** Both succeed (exit 0). The difference is exactly two warnings, on exactly the two files this PR touches.

`main`:

```
[plugin vite:resolve] Module "node:fs" has been externalized for browser compatibility,
imported by ".../src/data/naturalEarthRegions.js".
[plugin vite:resolve] Module "node:fs" has been externalized for browser compatibility,
imported by ".../src/data/neighborhoodPolygons.js".
```

This branch: no externalization warning at all.

That warning is not cosmetic. In `main`'s shipped bundle, `node:fs` becomes an empty frozen module:

```js
const i3=Object.freeze(Object.defineProperty({__proto__:null},Symbol.toStringTag,{value:"Module"}))
```

so `const { readFileSync } = await import('node:fs')` yields `undefined` and the next line calls it. Only the `isNode` guard stops that being a `TypeError` in production — which is the failure mode this PR removes rather than keeps guarding. This branch's bundle has 0 occurrences of `readFileSync` and 0 of `node:fs`.

The packs are bundled as lazy chunks and reachable from the index chunk: `assets/regions-*.js` (1.99 MB, contains `Pentecost` and `ne_10m_geography_regions_polys`), `assets/marine-*.js` (633 kB), `assets/san-francisco-*.js` (222 kB, contains `Bayview Hunters Point`).

One thing I hadn't noticed before building. On `main`, each pack ships **twice** — once as a JS chunk for the browser branch, and once as a raw `.json` asset, because the Node branch's `new URL('./local_data/.../x.json', import.meta.url)` makes Vite emit a URL asset too. Both sets are referenced from `main`'s index chunk. Removing the dual path drops the duplicates:

```
dist total:   30,536,517 B (main)  →  27,692,834 B (this branch)     −2.84 MB
dist/assets:  14,373,781 B         →  11,530,098 B
modules:      156                  →  152
```

So this also removes ~9% of the build output, which wasn't in the PR description.

Caveat on the numbers: I built on Node 22.15.1, below the declared `engines` floor of 24.14.0. Vite 6.4.3 built both branches fine and the comparison is apples-to-apples, but it isn't the declared runtime.

Answering the two questions from the thread:

**Reference implementation.** Two files to study, both on main:

- `src/data/earthquakes.js` (+ its `earthquakes.test.mjs`) — the house pattern for a keyless public-API layer: registration, polling, stats, credits, and what tests should cover. The header comment also shows the perf bar layers are held to.
- `src/mapStackController.js` (the Bing Labels path) — the imagery-overlay mechanics: a `Cesium.ImageryLayer` added and removed cleanly.

A weather layer is the marriage of the two — earthquakes' conventions plus the labels overlay's imagery handling. There's no existing imagery-overlay *data layer*, so this one becomes the reference for the next; worth getting the shape right.

**Performance envelope.** Your instinct is right: v1 = a single global composite frame, refreshed every ~30 minutes, one semi-transparent imagery layer. No time slider, no animation, no archive in v1 — that's where the perf risk lives, and it can come later behind the same layer id. For the satellite-imagery half, look at NASA GIBS (keyless WMTS, GOES/Himawari composites) — keyless-first is the project's direction; the next release boots with zero keys entirely.

Concrete review on #89.

Thanks for the PoC — the direction works: keyless source, single imagery layer, registry token, opt-in. Reviewed the diff (not run yet). Five things, four blocking:

1. **The tile URL is wrong — the layer can't render.** RainViewer's `weather-maps.json` returns per-frame `path` values that are opaque hashes now (e.g. `/v2/radar/b8ed988a56a2`), not timestamp-composed paths, and tile URLs also need the tile-size segment. Compose `host + frame.path + '/256/{z}/{x}/{y}/2/1_1.png'` from the API response instead of hardcoding a template around `{nowcastTime}`. (Checked against the live API today — substituting the timestamp 404s.)
2. **`destroy` throws.** `destroy: (viewer) => { this.disable(viewer) }` — an arrow function doesn't get the object's `this`, so `this.disable` is undefined and destroy raises a TypeError. Share a closure-level helper between `disable` and `destroy` instead.
3. **Registry tests.** The new `weather-radar` entry in `LAYER_STATE_REGISTRY` needs `src/data/layerState.test.mjs` updated to match — `npm test` fails as-is.
4. **Credits.** Every source registers in `src/data/dataCredits.js` and gets a row in `DATA_SOURCES.md` — house rule, and RainViewer's terms want visible attribution.
5. *(non-blocking)* Unit tests for the pure parts (latest-frame selection: happy/empty/error) in the style of `earthquakes.test.mjs`; bump `REFRESH_MS` to 30 min per the issue thread; add the missing trailing newline.

On not being able to run it: the next release boots fully keyless, so you'll be able to verify visually with zero setup. I'll put eyes on the rendering from this side once the fixes land.

Reviewed the diff — this is a quality contribution: registry + credits + DATA_SOURCES row, backoff, saturation reporting at the Overpass cap, abort-on-supersede, tests on the pure helpers. Thank you. I want this as the base for the ALPR layer.

Three more concrete items from a deeper pass on the data (all verified against live Overpass/taginfo today), to fold into the fix list:

1. **The exact-match filter misses a variant.** `["surveillance:type"="ALPR"]` skips the `camera;ALPR` semicolon-combo tagging (small but real — 61 nodes globally). Match it with a regex clause or a second selector.
2. **The 600-node cap saturates on a single city.** A half-degree box over Austin alone returns **669** ALPR nodes — above both `QUERY_LIMIT` (600) and `MAX_RENDERED` (500) — so a metro view silently truncates today. The saturation *reporting* you built is right; the ceilings need to rise (or density-decimate) so one city fits.
3. **The "336K+ worldwide" figure in the `DATA_SOURCES.md` row is wrong.** taginfo (data through 2026-08-28) puts `surveillance:type=ALPR` at **147,207** total. The 336K number appears to count `man_made=surveillance` broadly. Quote "~147K mapped worldwide (Aug 2026)" or, better, don't hardcode a number that ages.

Also for the record since I'm asking for changes: your `numTag('') === 0` fix — refusing to render a tagless camera as due north — is exactly right and should survive any refactor. `direction` coverage is 93.6% in the data, so the cones are the layer's best feature.

Follow-up context on the known limitation above (the five German metro anchors), so it does not hold up review of this PR.

I measured what a worldwide scan would actually yield — chunked by region, since a single global query gets a 504 from the mirror gateway at ~46 s regardless of the declared `[timeout:270]`:

| Region | tagged | usable |
|---|---|---|
| Europe West | 2000 (hit my own per-query cap — real number higher) | 920 |
| Europe East | 928 | 336 |
| Nordics | 468 | 294 |
| Oceania | 535 | 458 |
| North America East | 1092 | 228 |
| Africa + Asia | 146 | 9 |
| **Total** | **5169** | **2245** (1986 unique) |

66% carry a mapped `camera:direction`. Three regions returned 504 (North America West, South America, polar north), so worldwide is on the order of **~3000 usable cameras** — roughly 3× the current catalog, not a different order of magnitude.

**Why that is not this PR:** more cameras only help once the client stops draining the whole catalog. Measured in the running app with 924 cameras:

- 71 Cesium entities for the entire catalog — coverage geometry is already visible-set-only via `materializeCctvVisibleCoverageEntities`, so that part is fine
- `loading.loaded` reaches `total` at t=40 s, but `loading.active` only goes false at t=120 s — the tiles-ready pass re-enqueues the catalog while the counter is capped at `total`
- the real per-camera cost in the drain is `warmGroundFloor([point])` inside `updateRecordGeometry`, i.e. ~924 terrain resolutions

That second point is also, I believe, why `qa-cctv-v2`'s "geometry-load queue drains within Ns" assertion fails on a large catalog: the harness is right and the app's loading flag is wrong.

So the sequence I would suggest is: this PR as it stands → a viewport-scoped `/api/cctv/sources` (server keeps the full registry, client receives and drains only what is near the camera, so the frame proxy's registry contract and its SSRF hardening stay untouched) → worldwide chunks, which then also **deletes `OSM_WEBCAM_ANCHORS` entirely**, because with viewport scoping the per-pack cap no longer decides what a viewer sees.

Happy to open the viewport-scoping PR first if you would rather review them in that order — it stands on its own, since it cuts today's 803-camera drain just as much.

> 1. **Remove/gate `preserveDrawingBuffer: true`** — src/main.js:122

> 2. **Drop `msaaSamples: 4` to 2 or make it adaptive** — src/main.js:119
>    4× MSAA over Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles is one of the biggest fixed GPU costs per frame; brutal on integrated GPUs. Expose as a quality setting (the app already has a perf-investigation precedent for this pattern).
> 
> 3. **Cut the 58 `backdrop-filter: blur()` rules** — style.css (58 occurrences)
>    Every blurred HUD panel forces the compositor to read and blur the WebGL canvas beneath it *every frame*, and panels stack. Replacing with pre-baked translucent gradients/opaque backgrounds on the heaviest surfaces (command dock, trays, chips) is likely the single largest paint-cost win.
> 
> 4. **Replace the compass-tape `innerHTML` rebuild** — src/ui.js:1450-1457
>    On heading change it re-parses/rebuilds 7 `<span>`s via `innerHTML` string concat → parse + layout + GC churn during exactly the most interaction-heavy moments (camera motion). Build the strip once and slide it with a `transform: translateX` update (compositor-only).

 By connecting the API, your agent will read the exact structured JSON generated by the report. For our primary "God Modules" (like src/voice/gevActions.js, src/data/militaryFlights.js, and src/data/cctv.js), the engine has already generated specific skillContracts and dependencyShielding rules.

Tested this recipe on a Synology NAS (DSM 7, Docker 24, amd64): `npm ci` ~10 min on a Celeron, image 630 MB, ~1.25 GB RAM at rest, served behind DSM's reverse proxy plus a small Caddy TLS front so the mic works on iOS. Works well. Three notes worth a line in the README:

1. `user: "${UID:-1000}:${GID:-1000}"` — on DSM set it to the share owner explicitly (the DSM admin user is usually 1026:100), otherwise `.env` / `.gev-cache` end up owned by an unrelated uid.
2. When the port is published beyond loopback the Provider Settings panel is disabled by design, so keys go into `.env` by hand — fine, but worth saying next to the LAN note.
3. Copying the tree from macOS with `tar` ships `._*` AppleDouble files that `npm test` then picks up as test files (500+ spurious failures). `COPYFILE_DISABLE=1 tar …` fixes it; a `._*` line in `.dockerignore` would too.

## Data Extraction Analysis: LeoLabs Visualization

**Context**
Analysis of the LeoLabs LEO (Low Earth Orbit) visualization platform to determine the feasibility of exporting orbital data for use in external web visualizers.

**Diagnostics**
The application uses a modular plugin architecture to load specific orbital datasets and visualization logic. Technical findings regarding data sourcing and dependencies include:

| Resource Type | URL / Endpoint |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Data Assets Base** | `https://platform-assets.leolabs.space/visualization/` |
| **Static Data Key** | `static.json.gz` |
| **Platform API** | `https://platform.leolabs.space` |
| **CDN Base** | `https://platform-cdn.leolabs.space` |

**Actionable Findings**
*   **Orbital Propagation:** The site relies on `satellite.min.js` (SGP4/TLE propagation) and `geopack.min.js`. Data fetched is likely formatted specifically for these libraries (e.g., Two-Line Element sets).
*   **Authentication:** The presence of `window.userApiKeys` and `isLoggedIn` checks indicates that data access is protected by session-based or key-based authentication.
*   **CORS Restrictions:** Data resides on a specific assets subdomain (`platform-assets.leolabs.space`), which likely enforces Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) policies preventing direct browser-based fetches from external domains.
*   **State Management:** The visualization initializes via a `processMessage` function that handles settings like `reducedQuality` and `overflightModeEnabled`.

**Technical Recommendations**
To integrate similar orbital data into an external visualizer, consider the following strategies:

*   **Official API Access:** Utilize the [LeoLabs API](https://www.leolabs.space/) for authorized data retrieval rather than attempting to intercept internal visualization assets.
*   **Public TLE Sources:** For general satellite tracking, use the [Space-Track.org API](https://www.space-track.org), which provides industry-standard orbital data.
*   **Client-Side Libraries:** Implement the same propagation logic used in the source page to translate orbital elements into coordinates:


`````js

// as seen in the platform's dependency list.
import { twoline2satrec, propagate, gstime, eciToGeodetic } from 'satellite.js';

const satrec = twoline2satrec(tleLine1, tleLine2);
const positionAndVelocity = propagate(satrec, new Date());
const gmst = gstime(new Date());
const positionGeodetic = eciToGeodetic(positionAndVelocity.position, gmst);
`````

Separate layer is the right call, and for a reason worth writing down: the purpose is verifying what *your* antenna hears, and the moment that data is blended with an aggregator you can no longer answer "did my receiver get this?". So nothing below proposes merging the two by default.

What the issue leaves open is **overlap**: with both layers on, the same airframe is on the globe twice, at two positions, from two clocks. That's the one design decision here, and it's worth picking deliberately rather than finding it in review.

**Three defensible answers.** (1) *Draw both, always* — the issue's "visually distinguished". Honest and simplest; the cost is that in a dense receiver's coverage two markers for one plane at slightly different positions reads as a bug to anyone not thinking about provenance. (2) *Local wins where local has it* — Flights suppresses any ICAO the receiver is currently reporting with a fresh position, so one marker per airframe and the receiver's coverage becomes visible as the region where provenance switches. (3) *Local wins, and says so* — (2) plus a provenance field on the popup.

I'd suggest (1) as the default with (3) behind a toggle: keeps the layer independent as filed, and gives the dense-coverage case a way out. Worth flagging that (2)/(3) would be the first place in the tree where two sources are concurrently authoritative for the same object — OpenSky → adsb.lol is strict failover, one source at a time, and `src/data/adsbLolFallback.js` is a unit adapter rather than a merge. That's a precedent, not a pattern to follow.

**Receiver presence should be level-triggered.** A receiver isn't a feed that fails, it's a feed intermittently *there* — dongle unplugged, `readsb` restarted, USB power-saved. Infer presence from request outcomes and a restart mid-poll can wedge the layer in a state no later event clears. Deriving it from the data is self-correcting: `aircraft.json` carries a top-level `now` and per-aircraft `seen` / `seen_pos`. It also separates two things worth separating — "0 aircraft, antenna fine" is a valid answer, and only "receiver unreachable" is an error. `aisWatchdog.js` already draws exactly this distinction for AISStream (handshake ≠ liveness), including the split between when to *tell* the user and when to *act*.

**Staleness is per-aircraft here, not per-feed.** Every other live layer has one freshness number per snapshot; a receiver doesn't, because `seen_pos` is per airframe — some aircraft are 2s old and some 90s old and the feed is healthy. `getStats()` should say so, and a position past some `maxPositionAgeS` should drop rather than linger: an aircraft heard once at the edge of range otherwise ghosts on the globe until the layer is toggled off.

**On the credit governor.** I assumed a local receiver would let Flights poll less and save credits. It wouldn't — `/states/all` is global and costs a flat 4 credits per call regardless of viewport. The real interaction is better: during a 429 cooldown the proxy deliberately serves last-good with `X-OpenSky-Stale`, and a live receiver means there is genuinely fresh first-hand data for part of the view during exactly that window. Under (2)/(3) the cooldown degrades to "fresh where your antenna reaches, stale elsewhere" instead of uniformly stale — better failure mode, no budget change, no new upstream calls.

**One thing worth deciding up front:** which side fetches the receiver URL. Client-side keeps it a local-network concern. Server-side makes a user-supplied host an SSRF surface and puts it under SECURITY.md's "no arbitrary-URL fetching" rule. It changes the whole shape, so it's cheaper to choose now than to refactor later. Out of scope either way, I'd say: no writing to the receiver, no MLAT, and no persisting local traffic — that last one is a different feature with different privacy questions.

If #305's shared flight-tracking engine lands, this should plug into whatever ingestion seam it produces rather than re-implementing polling and marker lifecycle, so probably worth sequencing after it.

Happy to implement — but the overlap choice is a product call, so I'd rather a maintainer picked 1/2/3 than guess and send a large PR against the wrong one.

3. Whether `E:\Applications\Pinokio\api\gods-eye-view\src\main.js` exists.
4. The equivalent log from the Arch attempt.

**1. `ponytail:` markers.** Gone. You were right that it was a tooling artifact leaking through; I've stripped them and they won't be in future PRs.

**2. bbox quantization (#63, @d8ahazard).** Fetch boxes now snap to a 0.125° grid via `quantizeBox()`, credited to @d8ahazard in both the code and the commit. Three details worth flagging since they're judgement calls:

- **Snaps outward** (floor the low edges, ceil the high edges) rather than to nearest, so the fetch box always contains the viewport. Rounding to nearest would sometimes fetch a box smaller than what's on screen and leave a visible margin unpopulated.
- **Snaps after the viewport-size gate**, so the "zoom in" prompt still reflects the real viewport rather than the padded fetch box.
- **Panning inside a cell now skips the request entirely**, not just reuses the cache key. That's the bigger win, but it makes staleness a real risk, so the cached cell is cleared on a failed fetch and on `disable()` — otherwise an error or a disable/re-enable could serve a stale cell. `destroy()` routes through `disable()`.

I used `0.125` rather than #63's `0.14`: a power-of-two fraction is exactly representable, so grid lines never drift.

This replaces the original branch entirely: `vite.config.js` went from 7,995 lines to 3 while this sat open, so the proxy half had to be re-authored rather than rebased. It was also stacked on the OpenSeaMap and Radio→Voice work; that's untangled now and this is one tap on its own, as you asked.

## What it is

Rayhunter runs on a device the user owns — a flashed Orbic hotspot, reached over USB tether or its own Wi-Fi — and flags suspicious cellular behaviour. Its embedded web server sends no CORS headers, so the browser can't read it directly.

`server/providers/rayhunter.js` relays two read-only endpoints same-origin, registered in `local.js` like every other provider. GET only; nothing is ever written to the device.

## What changed versus the version you last saw

- **The address check is no longer ad-hoc.** The old `validBase()` accepted any host and blocklisted exactly one address, with a comment arguing the tradeoff. That's now `parseTapAddress()` from #382: loopback, RFC1918, or `.local`, and a public or malformed address is a 400 with **no upstream request made at all**. Both real access paths are private addresses, so this costs nothing in practice — I checked the branch's own default `192.168.1.1:8080` along with USB-tether, hotspot and iOS `172.20.10.x` ranges.
- **The client's hand-synced copy of the regex is gone.** It carried a comment saying it was kept in sync by hand across the trust boundary. Both sides now call the same function, which is why #382 puts the module in `src/data/` rather than under `server/providers/` — #274 is open about eight copies of haversine and I didn't want to add a ninth pattern.
- **Rate limit**, 120/min per client with a 600 global backstop. Not a quota guard, since the upstream is the user's own hardware — it stops a runaway client loop from wedging a small embedded web server.
- **8 MB streaming body cap, and redirects refused** rather than followed, so a device response can't walk the request outside the address that was just validated.
- **Upstream error text is no longer relayed to the browser** — logged locally, client is told only that the device is unreachable.

## Fixtures — the part I'd like you to look at

CI has no Rayhunter, so the proxy takes an injectable `fetchImpl` and the tests drive it from `src/data/fixtures/`. That matched an existing convention rather than needing a new harness, which is why #382 doesn't ship one.

**These fixtures are synthetic, written to the API shape in EFForg/rayhunter — not device captures, and they're labelled that way in the fixtures README.** I didn't want to put something in a file whose README documents provenance and quietly imply it came off hardware. They do exercise the cases the parser has to survive: the leading metadata line with no `events` array, `null` entries in the positional per-analyzer array, an `Informational` event that must be filtered, one of each real severity, and a trailing malformed line. A real capture would be strictly better and would need no test changes — I have the hardware and can swap one in if you'd rather.

## Honest limitation, unchanged

Warnings are plotted at **the browser's position when the warning is first observed, not the device's position at detection time** — the app has no way to know the latter. That's stated in `getStats().error`, `DATA_SOURCES.md` and the CURRENT-STATE section rather than presented as a precise fix.

## Also here

`DataLayerManager` grows a generic `chip.prompt` path so a layer row can carry a free-text setting instead of a static `params` object. The device address is its only consumer today, so I kept it here rather than in the contract PR; if #57 goes server-side it's already there.

## Verification

`npm test` 3000 pass / 0 fail with `GEV_REQUIRE_ALLOCATION_GATE=1` on Node 24.19.0, `npm run build` clean, `npm run test:track` 108 passed / 0 failed, `format:check` and `check:boundaries` clean.

11 new proxy tests cover the relay path, the SSRF refusals (public, link-local, hostname) asserting no upstream call is made, method gating, traversal-shaped recording names, unreachable devices, device HTTP errors, the rate limiter, redirect refusal, and the body cap. `DATA_SOURCES.md` and `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` are updated in the same commit.

Rebuilt on current main as a single commit. Independent of the tap-contract work in #382 — WiGLE is a fixed public API behind a token, not a user-addressed local device, so it needs none of that.

`vite.config.js` went from 7,995 lines to 3 while this sat open, so the proxy is re-authored as `server/providers/wigle.js` registered in `local.js`. It was also stacked on the OpenSeaMap branch; that's untangled and this is one layer on its own.

## Licensing — the part I'd want you to decide on

You confirm data terms yourself before a source lands (#256), so here's the text rather than my summary. WiGLE's [data licence](https://wigle.net/eula.html):

> **LICENSE GRANT.** …a non-exclusive right to use the maps and access point database (hereinafter, "the Data") **on a single computer (i.e., with a single CPU)**. You, or another person with your express permission and supervision, may also use the Data on any computer system owned by you at a single location provided you can: (1) **guarantee that there is no possibility of its use by more than one person at a time**; and, (2) that you do not receive any remuneration for the other person's use of the Data.

> **RESTRICTIONS.** You may not rent, lease, sublicense, transfer, **distribute, telecommunicate, copy**, or sell the Data in its entirety or in any part **for any commercial consideration, gain, or benefit**.

WiGLE's FAQ adds that money-making use requires a separate commercial licence with its own unthrottled tokens.

For the local open-source app this is fine, and it's what the layer is built for: each user brings their own account, so each user is the licensee under their own acceptance, and nothing is redistributed — no WiGLE data is committed, it's fetched at runtime and cached only on the machine that queried it under git-ignored `.gev-cache/`.

**Where it bites is the hosted version.** README line 502 says one is coming at Halfpixel. Single-computer, one-person-at-a-time, and no distribution for commercial benefit all point the same way: **this layer needs a commercial licence from WiGLE before it can ship in a hosted product, or it has to stay disabled there.** I've written that into DATA_SOURCES.md in the same shape as the Google News restriction already on the regional briefing, since that's the established precedent in that file. Happy to reword if you read the clauses differently — I'd rather you saw the quotes than my paraphrase.

## Hardening beyond the port

Re-reading the original turned up three things worth fixing:

- **Upstream message text was being relayed to the browser.** WiGLE answers HTTP 200 with `{success:false}` for several real failures, so status alone can't separate them. `wigleClientError()` now maps status to our own wording and keeps the three distinctions that change what the user should actually do — credentials rejected / allowance exhausted / everything else — and the upstream message is logged locally only. There's a test asserting a planted upstream string never reaches the client.
- **No rate limit, timeout, or body cap.** Now 60/min per client (300 global), 15s timeout, 4 MB cap, `redirect: 'manual'`.
- **A non-JSON body threw inside the handler.** Now a clean 502.

## Spending the allowance slowly

The per-account daily allowance is small, and that shapes everything: 0.4° viewport cap, 24h memory+disk cache keyed on the rounded bbox (access points don't move), in-flight coalescing so a burst of pans costs one query, and a soft daily counter defaulting to 50.

The counter reuses `normalizeBudget`/`isOverBudget` from `tomtomTiles.js` rather than a second hand-rolled copy, but rolls on `wiglePacificDayKey()` — WiGLE resets at US/Pacific midnight, not UTC. It's in-memory and resets on server restart; TomTom's persisted `budget.json` is the upgrade path if that proves insufficient.

## Fixture

Tests run offline against `src/data/fixtures/wigle-network-search.json`. **It's synthetic and labelled as such — deliberately containing no real observed network.** Real rows are other people's crowdsourced observations under the licence above, so committing any would be exactly the redistribution DATA_SOURCES says we don't do. It covers what the normalizer must handle: a current network, an aged one, blank `ssid`/`channel` (`Number('')` is `0`, so blank has to read as missing, not zero), and an untriangulated `0,0` row that must be dropped rather than plotted in the Gulf of Guinea.

## Verification

`npm test` 2990 pass / 0 fail with `GEV_REQUIRE_ALLOCATION_GATE=1` on Node 24.19.0, `npm run build` clean, `npm run test:track` 108 passed / 0 failed, `format:check` and `check:boundaries` clean. 11 new proxy tests plus the existing pure-helper tests.

`DATA_SOURCES.md`, `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md`, `SECURITY.md` and `.env.example` are updated in the same commit.

The new `createGeospatialServices()` abstraction looks like a good seam for one additional layer of provider composition. I’m thinking of three closely related additions that would remain within the scope of this PR:

1. **Provider provenance**
   Preserve normalized source metadata with geospatial results, e.g. provider, operation, attribution and retrieval time. This would let downstream consumers distinguish where a result originated without exposing provider-specific response objects.

2. **Capability/provider registry**
   Introduce a small registry/descriptor layer so providers can explicitly declare their supported operations and metadata, while keeping the current `providers.{reverseGeocode,textSearch,nearby,route}` API backward-compatible. 3. **Explicit fallback composition**
   Add a small utility for composing providers in a caller-selected order. I would keep all three deliberately small and test-driven:

* no changes to tool schemas;
* no request-controlled upstream URLs;
* no hidden provider retries;
* existing provider behavior remains the default;
* existing normalized result contracts remain intact.

Contributor review, not a maintainer verdict. Checked against `main` at `a8125ad`; this one still merges clean.

**The span bug is real and the fix for it is correct.** At HEAD, `bounds.east - bounds.west` for a box straddling ±180° is about `-359.96`, so `Math.min(-359.96, 0.05)` keeps the negative value and the returned box is inverted with a ~360° span. `longitudeSpanDeg` fixes that, and the `((lon + 540) % 360) - 180` wrap is the right idiom.

**But normalizing `west`/`east` on the way out moves the failure into the callers rather than removing it.** `clampBoundsAroundCenter` has two call sites, both in `src/layers/traffic/viewport.js:167` and `:213`, and the returned box immediately feeds three consumers that all assume `west <= east`:

`getBoundsCenter` (`viewport.js:97`) is a plain mean:

```js
lon: (bounds.west + bounds.east) / 2,
```

For the test's own input the PR returns `west = 179.97, east = -179.99`, so the center comes out at **`-0.01` instead of `179.98`** — off by ~180°, about 20 000 km. That value is the `center` passed to `distanceKm(center, layerState._lastViewCenter)` in the `MIN_CENTER_SHIFT_KM` gate and is then stored as `_lastViewCenter`, so the fetch gate is comparing a point on the opposite side of the planet.

Worth being precise about the trade here: the *pre-PR* code, broken as its box is, gets the center right by accident — `(west + east) / 2` with the symmetric inverted span collapses back to `center.lon`. So this specific value regresses.

`boundsOverlap` (`viewport.js:134`) degenerates twice over: `overlapE = Math.min(a.east, b.east)` against `overlapW = Math.max(a.west, b.west)` trips the `overlapE <= overlapW` early return, and `aArea = (a.north - a.south) * (a.east - a.west)` is negative so `aArea > 0` fails. The overlap skip therefore never fires near the antimeridian and every camera change re-fetches — extra Overpass load in exactly the region the PR is trying to fix.

Third, `loadRoadsForBounds` turns the box into an Overpass bbox, which needs `west < east`.

**The test passes while the caller is broken**, which is the part I'd flag hardest. It asserts the wrapped span and that both edges are in `[-180, 180)` — both true — but not the property the callers depend on. A test asserting `getBoundsCenter(result)` lands near `179.98` would fail on this patch, and that is the assertion that would have caught it.

**Two ways forward, and I'd suggest the first:**

*Scope it to the span.* Keep `longitudeSpanDeg`, drop `normalizeLonDeg` from the return. You get `west = 179.97, east = 180.01` — outside the conventional range, but monotonic, so the span is right, `getBoundsCenter` returns `179.99`, and `boundsOverlap` keeps working. A clean, small, honest fix; the remaining "coordinates exceed 180" issue is then one visible problem at the Overpass boundary instead of a wrong number flowing through the gate logic.

*Or make the whole path cyclic* — a wrap-aware longitude midpoint in `getBoundsCenter`, seam splitting in `boundsOverlap`, and a bbox that Overpass accepts. That's the complete fix, but it's a different and much larger PR, and I'd want the maintainers to say whether traffic at the antimeridian is worth that before anyone writes it.

Either way the `longitudeSpanDeg` helper and its docstring are keepers.

I agree with the core finding in this issue: the repository needs a shared geospatial foundation. The duplicated implementations, inconsistent constants/units, and especially the `(lon, lat)` vs `(lat, lon)` argument-order mismatch in `naturalEarthRegions.js` make that a correctness and maintainability problem rather than merely duplicated code.

#287 addresses a substantial part of this correctly by introducing a shared `greatCircleKm()` / `greatCircleMeters()` primitive and migrating the existing consumers. The Natural Earth migration also correctly removes the specific swapped-coordinate call pattern identified here.

However, I think the current approach leaves two important parts of the contract unresolved:

**1. The coordinate contract is documented but not strongly represented by the API.**

The new primitive uses four positional numbers:

```js
greatCircleKm(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2)
```

That is an improvement over having multiple inconsistent conventions, but it still permits the exact class of silent coordinate-order error that motivated this issue. JavaScript cannot distinguish latitude from longitude when both are plain numbers.

An object-based contract such as:

```js
greatCircleMeters(
  { lat, lon },
  { lat, lon },
)
```

would make the coordinate semantics explicit and would also provide a natural place for finite/range validation.

I’m not saying the positional API cannot work; rather, I think #274 should explicitly decide whether the canonical contract is only a documented convention or something we want the API itself to make harder to misuse.

**2. A canonical geodesic primitive and spatial-query semantics are different layers.**

The current consolidation establishes:

```text
point + point → distance
```

But #188 is deliberately concerned with:

```text
collection + center + radius → ordered matches
collection + point → nearest entity
entity → position accessor
deterministic tie behavior
invalid-position handling
```

I think these should remain separate abstractions rather than trying to make the geodesic utility responsible for both.

My preferred structure would therefore be:

```text
#274
canonical geodesic primitive
        ↓
#188
spatial-query primitive
        ↓
domain consumers
```

This would allow CCTV, traffic, aircraft, vessels, regions, etc. to share the same spatial-selection semantics without coupling the utility to any particular entity shape.

There is also one small numerical compatibility point in the current #287 migration worth resolving explicitly: `src/voice/gevActions.js` previously used a radius of `6371.0088 km`, while the new shared primitive uses `6371 km`. The numerical difference is very small, but this means that particular migration is not strictly behavior-preserving and should either retain the previous canonical value or explicitly accept/document the standardization.

I also think the test surface of the new primitive should establish the canonical contract independently of the consumer migrations: at minimum identity, small-distance calibration, dateline crossing, antipodal points, symmetry, invalid-coordinate behavior, and the coordinate-order contract.

I’m not proposing that #188 replace this issue or that every existing consumer be migrated again. I think the cleaner outcome is for #274 to establish the lower-level geodesic contract, while #188 builds the higher-level reusable spatial-query semantics on top of it.

That would give the repository a distinction between:

```text
geodesic mathematics
        ↓
spatial query / selection
        ↓
domain-specific geometry
```

while still allowing intentional local approximations, such as the existing traffic viewport calculation, to remain local when they are solving a different problem.

Not a review of this PR's architecture — just field notes from having taken the
interface all the way through one language, in case they are useful while the
locale core is still being shaped.

I maintain an out-of-tree Simplified Chinese layer for my own use. I'm aware
from #412 and #312 that an automatic DOM translator is not the path being
selected, and I'm not proposing one here. But whichever catalog design lands,
these four places will bite, because they are not "a string in a template":

**1. Three labels use their own text as animation state.**
`setSplitFlapText` treats `element.textContent` as the settled value
(`src/splitFlap.js:456`), and `settle()` bails when it no longer matches
(`src/splitFlap.js:424`). Any layer that changes the text of
`#global-loading-label`, `#traffic-sync-label` or `#cctv-sync-label` after the
app sets it will re-trigger the cascade on every ticker cycle. A catalog that
resolves the string *before* `setSplitFlapText` is called is fine; one that
rewrites afterwards is not.

**2. Two summaries are typed in character by character.**
`src/hud.js:674` and `src/ui/cctvPresentation.js:213` both do
`textContent = text.slice(0, i)` on an interval, so every frame is a different
string. Same rule: localize the source string, not the element.

**3. The HUD summary is composed from DOM text.**
`src/hud.js:630` reads `#hud-mode`'s `textContent` back to build the summary
line. Localize the mode chip without localizing the composition and you get one
translated word in front of a line of English telemetry.

**4. Four Material Symbols ligature names are also real UI labels.**
The icon font renders the element's *text*, so `draw`, `normal`, `radio` and
`adjust` must never be looked up as copy — while `Draw`, `Normal`, `RADIO` and
`ADJUST` are genuine labels a few lines away. `display-controls.html:94-95` is
the clearest case: the ligature and the label are adjacent lines in the same
component. Any case-insensitive key lookup will turn an icon into a word, and
`index.html`'s `icon_names` list is the authoritative set to exclude.

One non-obvious presentation note: the console's labels carry 1.4–1.6px / 0.16em
tracking (e.g. `src/ui/styles/layers.css:323`, `command-dock.css:130`). That
reads as precision in Latin small caps and as broken spacing in CJK, where every
glyph already has its own side bearings. A locale probably needs a tracking hook,
not just strings.

Happy to contribute the Simplified Chinese terminology once a catalog shape is
settled — ~400 reviewed entries plus the set of strings that should deliberately
*stay* English (MGRS/GSD/NIIRS-style imagery-intel abbreviations, unit symbols,
provider names and map attribution). That data is architecture-independent, so
just say the word and the format.

## Verified end to end

Ran a real Washington-state import and drove the app against it. Results:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Direct query, downtown Seattle bbox | 1633 elements, **0.56 s** |
| Same query through `/api/overpass` | 1633 elements, **3.1 s** cold, `X-Overpass-Cache: HIT` warm |
| Serving endpoint | `X-Overpass-Upstream: http://localhost:12345/api/interpreter` |
| Street Traffic layer | `mode: "live"`, `LIVE · TomTom flow · 82% cov`, **2617 dots**, `error: null` |
| Flow buckets | free 2140 · slow 12 · jam 0 · sim 465 |

For contrast, the same query against the public mirrors from this machine takes **45 s to fall through all four and return an Apache 406 error page**.

Named roads came back correct for the bbox — Montlake Boulevard NE, Ship Canal Bridge, Mount Baker Ridge Tunnel — so this is real geometry, not a shape that merely parses.

### Two first-run defects this surfaced

Both are in the compose file and both only appear on a genuine first import, which is why they are worth calling out rather than folding in silently:

1. **`/db` is the `overpass` user's home directory**, so a fresh named volume inherits its `0700` mode. The import runs as `overpass` and reports success, but the CGI process answering queries runs as a different user and cannot traverse `/db` to reach the dispatcher socket. Every query fails with `runtime error: open64: 13 Permission denied /db/db//osm3s_osm_base` while the logs say initialization completed — a healthy-looking container serving nothing.
2. **Overriding `entrypoint` clears the image's CMD**, which the image's own entrypoint needs as its argument. Without restating it the container exits 0 and restarts forever with empty logs.

Fixed in 676daf0 and documented in the troubleshooting section.

### Note on `scripts/qa-traffic-baseline.mjs`

It cannot validate a regional instance: it primes a hardcoded **Austin** viewport, which is outside a Washington extract, so the empty-rotates-as-refusal guard correctly declines and the harness times out waiting for dots. That is the guard working as designed rather than a regression — but it does mean the harness assumes planet-wide Overpass coverage, which may be worth parameterising separately.

I independently hit the same unbounded-cache problem (from the #327 angle) and wrote a fix before finding this PR. Yours is broader — coordinate validation, the disk byte cap and the rate limiter are all things I didn't do — so rather than open a competing PR I'd rather hand you what I found. One of these is a real edge case in the current implementation; the other is a suggestion.

## Eviction runs before the response is rebuilt, and can drop a hit the request still needs

`evictTerrainCache(cache, maxCacheEntries)` is called inside the `missing.length > 0` block, after the insert loop but **before** `const results = requested.map(...)` reads the cache back. Eviction sorts by `at`, which is only ever set at fetch time, so a long-cached point sorts first even when the current request is reading it.

The docstring says "a point refreshed during the current request is never the one dropped", which is true — refreshed points carry `at = fetchedAt` and sort last. But a **cache hit** carries its original old `at` and is fully eligible.

Reproduced against your `evictTerrainCache` verbatim, cap of 3:

```
cache: hot(at=1), b(at=50), c(at=60)
request: ['hot' (hit), 'new' (miss)]

insert 'new' -> evict -> rebuild

cache after evict : b, c, new
hot point survived: false
rebuilt results   : [null, {"ellipsoid":9}]
```

The null makes `resolveTerrainHeightRequest` return 502 for a request every point of which was satisfiable. Reachable once the cache is at cap: `hot` here stands in for something like a fixed CCTV or installation position resolved once at startup and re-read constantly afterwards — the oldest `at` in the map, and so the first victim, despite being the hottest entry.

Two ways to close it, either is small:
- move the `evictTerrainCache` call after the `results` rebuild, or
- skip keys in `unique` when choosing victims.

## Sorting by fetch time evicts hot entries first

Same root cause, separate from the 502. Because `at` is never updated on read, the eviction order is "least recently *fetched*", not "least recently *used*". The entry read every frame is exactly the one with the oldest `at`, so it gets evicted while a cold point fetched a minute ago and never touched again survives.

Touching an entry on read makes `Map` insertion order a real LRU and lets eviction be `cache.keys().next()` — which also drops the `[...cache.entries()].sort()` (O(n log n) plus a 50k-element array copy on each fetching request) down to O(1):

```js
function touch(cache, key) {
  const entry = cache.get(key);
  if (entry === undefined) return entry;
  cache.delete(key);
  cache.set(key, entry);
  return entry;
}
```

Called where the freshness loop already does `cache.get(key)`. Worth touching on *any* existing entry rather than only fresh ones, since the final rebuild serves stale-but-valid entries too.

This is the same `Map`-insertion-order trick already used by `memSet` in `server/providers/traffic.js` and `trimOverpassCache` in `server/providers/overpass/cache.js`, so it matches existing house style.

## Offer

I have both of these implemented with four regression tests, including one that fails with a 502 against a working-set-unaware evictor. Happy to push them to your branch, open a PR against it, or just paste the diff here — whichever you prefer. Equally happy to leave it entirely; you got here first and it's your patch.

One unrelated note in case it's useful: #327's title points at `src/services/terrainHeights.js`, the client-side cache, which looks like #594's territory rather than this PR's server-side one. Might be worth a cross-reference so the two don't get deduped by mistake.

You asked on #333 for current-main profiling and a measured frame-time comparison before accepting perf changes, so here are measurements of the suggestions in this issue on real integrated graphics. Two of the top three don't survive measurement on my hardware, and the biggest lever isn't listed.

**Rig:** Windows 11, Intel UHD 770 (ANGLE / D3D11), i7-12700T, 16 GB. Chrome headed, real GPU (not SwiftShader). Canvas 1264x705, keyless Esri basemap, no data layers enabled, parked camera, warm tile cache.

**Method, and one trap worth flagging.** Frames are counted from `scene.postRender`, not from rAF ticks, and every arm asserts the canvas dimensions are unchanged. I mention this because my first pass measured rAF and reported a clean 60 fps for "HUD hidden" — rendering had silently stopped and rAF was just free-running. Any perf number here that isn't tied to a verified render count and a verified canvas size is not trustworthy. Arms are interleaved A/B/A over 4 rounds with the order reversed on alternate rounds, so tile-cache warming and thermal drift hit every arm equally.

## Results (median rendered fps, 4 interleaved rounds)

| Arm | fps | vs shipped |
|---|---|---|
| as shipped (msaa 4, scale 1.0) | 17.9 | — |
| **msaa 2** (item 2) | 20.5 | **+15%** |
| **msaa 1** (item 2) | 29.6 | **+65%** |
| backdrop-filter: none (item 3) | 18.9 | +6% |
| **resolutionScale 0.75** | 26.3 | **+47%** |
| **resolutionScale 0.5** | 35.6 | **+99%** |
| msaa 1 + scale 0.5 + no blur | 46.5 | +160% |

Sample spreads were tight (e.g. msaa 1: 29.1, 29.3, 29.8, 29.6), so the large effects are real and the small ones are genuinely small.

## Item 2 (MSAA) is correct and is the biggest listed win

+65% going 4 -> 1, +15% going 4 -> 2. This is the one item I'd act on as-is. A middle setting is viable if 4x is wanted on capable GPUs.

## Item 1 (preserveDrawingBuffer) shows no measurable effect

Flipped `preserveDrawingBuffer` to `false` in `src/app/viewer.js` and re-ran the whole matrix. Baseline went 17.9 -> 18.2 fps, with overlapping samples (`true`: 18.9, 16.8, 17.9, 17.7 / `false`: 18.2, 17.0, 17.1, 18.3). Two independent runs agreed. The reasoning in the issue is sound in general, but on this driver/compositor path it isn't costing anything measurable. Still might be worth gating on principle — just not as a perf win.

## Item 3 (backdrop-filter) is real but small

+6% in one run, -1% in another, i.e. at the edge of noise — not "the single largest paint-cost win". I also tested hiding overlay containers one at a time and no single element moved the needle; the HUD cost is diffuse and modest, not concentrated.

Note the count is now 64 occurrences across `src/ui/styles/*.css`, not 58 in `style.css`.

## The unlisted lever: resolutionScale

`viewer.resolutionScale` is never set anywhere in the tree, so it runs at full device pixel ratio. It's the strongest single knob here: 0.5 nearly doubles frame rate, and it stacks with MSAA for +160% combined.

Scaling is sub-linear, which is informative. Fitting frame time against pixel count across scales 1.0 / 0.75 / 0.5 / 0.35 / 0.25 gives roughly **22 ms fixed + 40 ms per megapixel**. So there's a ~22 ms per-frame floor on this hardware that no resolution reduction touches, capping this machine near ~44 fps even at trivial resolutions. During that floor the JS main thread is idle 72% of the time and the Cesium render phase measures ~11 ms, so the remainder is outside JS and outside `scene.render()` — compositor/present path. I could not reduce it.

## Stale references

Some of this issue predates a refactor: `src/main.js` is now 17 lines and the viewer options live in `src/app/viewer.js`; `style.css` is 21 lines with the CSS split under `src/ui/styles/`. Item 5 (splitting the monolithic stylesheet) looks already done.

## Suggestion

If you want it, the shape the data supports is a quality preset that sets `msaaSamples` and `resolutionScale` together, defaulting conservatively on low-end GPUs — that combination is the +160%, and everything else here is noise by comparison. Happy to open a PR for that, or to just leave the numbers. I have the harness if a reproduction on other hardware would help; worth noting n=1 machine, so the fixed-cost floor in particular may be specific to this iGPU.

I found a fix for the live Street Traffic issue on my setup.

### Fix

In `server/providers/overpass/constants.js`, I removed `overpass.osm.ch` from the `OVERPASS_UPSTREAMS` list and used these mirrors instead:

```js
const OVERPASS_UPSTREAMS = [
  'https://overpass.kumi.systems/api/interpreter',
  'https://overpass.private.coffee/api/interpreter',
  'https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter',
  'https://lz4.overpass-api.de/api/interpreter',
];
```

After restarting the server, live traffic started working immediately and I could see the traffic moving on the map.

### What was happening

With `overpass.osm.ch` first in the list, the server received HTTP 200 responses, but the Overpass response contained:

```json
"elements": []
```

The traffic console consequently reported:

`Loaded major: 0 dots (roads=0...)`

and

`Loaded full: 0 dots (roads=0...)`

TomTom itself was working correctly — the TomTom traffic `.pbf` requests returned HTTP 200 and the app reported:

`TomTom key present — live flow mode`

So it appears the issue is that `overpass.osm.ch` can return a successful response while providing no road elements for the requested area. Removing that mirror (or making the proxy detect an unexpectedly empty result and try another mirror) fixed the traffic layer for me.

Hopefully this helps reproduce and fix the issue for other users.

Each of these proxies was written with real care about the **upstream** — validate the target, cap the body, cache the answer, honour a cooldown. What none of them bounded was **the caller**. On the root cause — this one is not the rate-limit family the other open reports share, it is a diagnosis failure:

The Street Traffic layer has **two independent upstreams**: OpenStreetMap, through `/api/overpass`, for road geometry, and TomTom for flow. Only one of them can be down at a time. But the failure path collapsed both into a single line — `Road data temporarily unavailable` — and that line is the wrong shape for the situation it describes. It reads like a configuration problem, and the only configuration this layer has is the TomTom key. So the reader goes and checks their key, which is the half that was working, and loses the afternoon to it. That is exactly the report in #661: *working TomTom access, still says road data unavailable.*

The real cause was upstream of the key entirely — the Overpass mirror refusing the query — and the panel had no way to say so.

So the change is not a new behaviour, it is the layer telling the truth about which half failed:

- `Overpass rate-limited` (429)
- `Overpass timed out` (504)
- `Overpass refused the road query (HTTP <code>)` for anything else
- `Overpass temporarily unavailable` when the adapter hands back a refusal with no status on it — because `HTTP undefined` on a panel row is worse than not naming a number

The status travels *beside* the message as well as inside it (`RoadRequestError.status`), so a caller can branch on the code without parsing English — the same shape `LiveSourceError` already uses in `src/sources/live/contract.js`. The first two strings match `alpr`'s Overpass source word for word; this is the project's existing vocabulary, not a new one.

Two things it deliberately does **not** claim:

- It does not say the road data is gone. Anything the browser did not classify keeps the original general line, because a raw platform `e.message` is not a sentence anyone should have to read off a panel.
- It does not say how many mirrors were tried. The proxy rotates mirrors behind `/api/overpass`; a refusal arriving in the browser means the proxy had nothing better to offer, and how it got there is not something this side knows. The message does not pretend otherwise.

On the root cause — this one is not the rate-limit family the other open reports share. It is a **mismatch between two shapes that were each individually correct**:

Roads are *fetched* in a square box centred on the look-at ground point. The frame is a *camera rectangle*. At a level pitch those two nearly agree, so nothing looks wrong. At an oblique pitch they stop agreeing badly: a large part of every fetched tile sits outside the frame, much of it behind the camera. The dot allocator was then doing exactly what it was written to do — spread `MAX_DOTS` fairly across the roads it was given — and fairness across the *tile* is the wrong objective when the budget is a *screen* budget. The result is a cap spent on geometry the user cannot see, and it is invisible in the code because neither half is wrong on its own.

So the change is not a new policy, it is giving the allocator the frame it was always implicitly serving: roads inside the camera rectangle plus a margin ring reach their ideal count first, and everything else takes what the visible tier leaves.

Three things I would put in front of a reviewer, because they are the parts I would want to argue with:

**There is a real trade, and it is in the fairness seed.** When the cap is too small to give every road one dot, the seed now goes to the visible roads — so a road *outside* the frame can drop to zero dots where it previously kept one. That is the intended direction, but it is a loss, not a free win, and it should be stated as one.

**The margin ring is floored at `MIN_CENTER_SHIFT_KM`, and that floor is load-bearing.** `onCameraChanged` skips reloading — and therefore skips re-allocating — for any pan shorter than that distance. I went through this one against the current tree (`082074a`) and against the raw OurAirports data before writing anything, because three of the assumptions in the issue body turn out to be load-bearing and two of them don't survive contact with the data. Everything below is measured or read, not guessed — file:line so you can check me.

---

## 1. `type` in `airport-frequencies.csv` is not flight phase, and most airports have no tower to hear

I downloaded today's `airports.csv` (13 MB, 86,119 rows) and `airport-frequencies.csv` (1.3 MB, 30,348 rows) and counted:

| | airports |
|---|---|
| have **any** frequency at all | 11,202 |
| have at least one TWR/GND/APP/ATIS-class frequency | 9,517 |
| have **all four** of GND + TWR + APP + ATIS | **521** |
| whose only air-ground frequency is CTAF / UNICOM / AFIS | **5,904** |

Per-type rows: TWR 3,437 (3,268 airports) · CTAF 3,250 · UNIC 2,938 · MISC 2,215 · APP 1,861 (1,689) · A/D 1,725 · GND 1,657 (1,606) · ATIS 1,588 (1,554) · RDO 1,558 · CNTR 1,211 · AFIS 1,065 · AWOS 1,011.

Also: 28,444 of the 30,348 rows parse into the 108–137 MHz VHF air band. **1,904 do not** — HF, UHF military, ranges written as text, blanks. Those need dropping at curation time or they'll render as plausible-looking garbage.

Two consequences for the design:

- The phase mapping in the issue (taxi→GND, takeoff/landing→TWR, cruise→CNTR/APP, approach→ATIS) only has all four rails at **521 airports worldwide**. Everywhere else the feature has to degrade, and the honest degradation is a sentence, not a silent fallback: *"Shannon (EINN) — tower 130.950. No ground or ATIS published."*
- For 5,904 airports the truthful answer is **"uncontrolled field — CTAF 122.800, pilots self-announce, no controller."** That's a real and interesting thing to teach a viewer, and it's the majority case. A design that assumes a tower exists will quietly lie at most of the world's airfields.

I'd suggest the pack carry the frequency *class* verbatim and let the UI say what's published, rather than promising a phase→frequency map it can only honour at 5% of airports.

## 2. Don't bundle OurAirports raw — the house already has a contract for this

`src/data/local_data/` is already 9.6 MB (`natural_earth` 2.6M, `datacenters` 2.5M, `cctv_ground_heights` 2.0M, `dams` 1.5M, `telegeography_submarine_cables` 1.1M, `neighborhoods` 228K). Adding 14.3 MB of CSV would more than double it.

The established pattern is a curated pack: `src/data/local_data/<name>/` + a `README.md` recording source dataset, exact upstream commit, fetch timestamp, license, curation parameters and feature counts — see `src/data/local_data/natural_earth/README.md`, which even states the budget line ("7.3 MB source → 2.5 MB pack (budget ≤3 MB, enforced by `src/data/naturalEarthRegions.test.mjs`)"). Loaded lazily (`src/data/naturalEarthRegions.js:129-134`):

```js
await import('./local_data/natural_earth/regions.json', { with: { type: 'json' } })
```

and the budget is a real gate (`src/data/naturalEarthRegions.test.mjs:98-101`).

I built the strawman pack to see whether it fits: idents + names + lat/lon + the four phase-relevant frequency classes, band-filtered, minified JSON → **1.11 MB**. That's inside the demonstrated house budget and lazy-loadable, so it costs nothing until someone tracks an aircraft.

## 3. The seam to read is `getTrackedInfo()`, not `viewer.trackedEntity`

#255 polls `viewer.trackedEntity` on a timer. The layer already publishes a proper seam: `flights.getTrackedInfo()` (`src/layers/flights/queries.js:840`) and `getTrackedSubject()` (`:853`), both already consumed by `src/cockpitMath.js:251-252` for civil and military contacts. Reading that instead keeps ATC out of Cesium internals and gets tracking-state changes for free.

Two useful things about what it already carries:

- It gives `latitude`, `longitude`, `altitudeM`, `onGround`, `velocityMps`, `track` — and a plausibility-gated `route: { origin: {code,name,lat,lon}, destination: {...} }`. The adsbdb enrichment already resolves airport **coordinates** (`server/providers/aircraft/enrichment.js:44-53`), so "nearest airport for the phase you're in" doesn't need a new lookup for the two airports that actually matter.
- It does **not** carry `verticalRateMps`, which any climb/descent classifier needs. That's not missing data — `info.verticalRate` is already in the record (`src/layers/flights/records.js:224`) and `mapAnalystRecord` surfaces it as `verticalRateMps` (`src/layers/flights/queries.js:248`). `_describeFlight` just doesn't pass it through. One line, and the field arrives on the seam already tested elsewhere.

And for "nearest airport": please reuse `greatCircleKm` from `src/data/routePlausible.js:17` rather than adding another haversine — 23 non-test files already carry one, which is the substance of #274/#188.

## 4. "Plays through the Radio transport, one audio source at a time" — there is no such transport yet

This is the part I'd most want settled before code lands, because it's the one that's cheap now and expensive later.

Radio's "one source at a time" guarantee isn't a shared contract. It's the incidental consequence of there being exactly one `HTMLAudioElement`, owned privately by Radio's own layer state: `layerState._audio = new Audio()` at `src/layers/radio/playback.js:36`, reachable only from inside that layer. Nothing outside Radio can ask "is audio free?" or "who has it?"

Meanwhile the app already has **eight** independent audio producers in `src/`: `voice/realtimeInput.js`, `voice/realtimeFacade.js`, `layers/radio/playback.js`, `layers/radio/tuningNoise.js`, `layers/cctv/videoPlayback.js`, `layers/cctv/projection.js`, `layers/weather/clock.js`, `data/bhoteKoshiEvent.js`. The only arbitration between any of them is Radio's one-way voice duck (`layerState._voiceDucked`, `src/layers/radio/volume.js:41-113`, applied as `_voiceDucked ? 0 : _userVolume`).

So ATC as written becomes a ninth producer, and "one audio source at a time" would be a comment rather than a mechanism — CCTV audio, the Bhote Koshi event and an ATC stream can all sound at once today.

The repo already has the right precedent for exactly this shape, one layer up: `src/data/inputOwnership.js` — `claimPointer(owner)` returns an opaque lease, `releasePointer(lease)`, plus `pointerOwner()` / `isPointerFree()` / `isPointerOwnedBy(owner)`. An audio equivalent (`claimAudio('atc')` / `releaseAudio(lease)`) would make the issue's sentence true for Radio, ATC **and** the six producers that predate both, and it's small. Without it, "one at a time" is enforced only by ATC choosing to route through Radio's private element — which works, but ties the two layers together and leaves the other seven unarbitrated.

Either way, ATC also has to join the two gates Radio already respects: `radioPresentationAllowed()` (`src/layers/radio/interaction.js:87`, gates on manager lifecycle `enabled` and not `uncertain`) and the `_voiceDucked` duck, so talking to the assistant ducks the tower the same way it ducks the music.

## 5. User-pasted stream URL

Agreed on shipping no LiveATC URLs. For the paste-your-own path, `src/layers/cctv/model.js:170-181` is the pattern already in the tree: the safe-`localStorage` accessor there guards the fact that *property access itself* can throw `SecurityError` under some privacy settings, not just `getItem`. Worth copying rather than re-deriving. Validate `https:` only at paste time (an `http:` stream is a mixed-content failure the user can't diagnose from the UI).

## 6. Attribution

New source ⇒ `DATA_SOURCES.md` **and** `src/data/dataCredits.js` (the file says so in its own header: "if you add a data source, add it there AND here"), with `src/data/dataCredits.test.mjs` as the gate. OurAirports is public domain, so the entry is short — but the *pack* README still needs the fetch timestamp and curation parameters, because unlike the upstream repos the others cite, OurAirports is a live-edited database with no commit to pin.

## 7. On #255 as the starting point

Worth flagging: #255 is currently `mergeable=false` / `dirty` against base `7596522`, +3,231 lines across 17 files. Between its base and today the tree moved a long way. If you want it as the base, it'll need a rebase before anything can be judged on it; and its client-side direct-stream note reads against the "no LiveATC stream URLs shipped" line in this issue, so that part needs rewriting regardless.

I’d like to propose a path forward for [#738], but before diving into implementation I’d love to get your thoughts on the architectural direction below.

My preference would be to avoid implementing Moon and Mars as isolated special-case layers. Instead, #738 could establish a small world/body context abstraction so that Earth remains the default while Moon and Mars can become first-class worlds within the same application architecture.

Initial concept:
Proposed WorldContext Abstraction:
Body: Active body identifier (earth, moon, mars)
Shape Model: Ellipsoid / surface geometry
Rotation Model: Reference frames and body-fixed transforms
Terrain & Imagery: Body-specific heightmaps and basemaps
Capabilities: Supported layer types and spatial features
Data Providers: Ephemeris, satellite, and mission data pipelines

The first implementation would not attempt to support every lunar or Martian dataset. The goal would be to establish the architectural seam cleanly and then build the data/layer support on top of it.

The initial slice I have in mind is:

1. **World-aware scene and camera state**
   Make the active world explicit and keep Earth as the default.

2. **Capability-based layers**
   Let layers declare which worlds/bodies they support rather than assuming Earth globally.

3. **Surface vs. orbital objects**
   Keep a clean distinction between surface assets such as rovers and orbital assets such as spacecraft.

4. **Data-provider boundary**
   Separate application-facing object/state contracts from providers such as Earth TLE data, JPL/Horizons ephemerides, and later higher-fidelity SPICE or mission-specific sources.

5. **Incremental implementation**
   Establish the world/context architecture first, then add Moon/Mars terrain, imagery, spacecraft, rover positions, and temporal trajectories in separate PRs.

Would you be comfortable with this proposed direction for #738, or would you prefer a narrower/different first architectural slice?

I’m ready to take this on once the architectural direction is agreed, with the implementation divided into small, reviewable PRs.

I spent a while measuring what this would actually cost against `f913066`, because
the interesting part turned out not to be the globe. Numbers below are from that
commit; the counts exclude test files.

## What Cesium already gives you

Better than I expected. The installed Cesium is **1.138** (the `^1.124.0` range has
floated up), and in that version:

- `Ellipsoid.MOON` and `Ellipsoid.MARS` are both built in — `MARS` is documented as
  a sphere at Mars' mean radii, sourced from EPSG:104905.
- `Ellipsoid.default` is a **settable** static (`WGS84`, `MOON`, `MARS` are
  `readonly`; `default` is not). The doc example is literally
  `Cesium.Ellipsoid.default = Cesium.Ellipsoid.MOON` followed by the Apollo 11
  landing site.
- `EllipsoidTerrainProvider` works against whatever ellipsoid is current, so a
  smooth Moon or Mars costs nothing.

What does *not* carry over: `createGooglePhotorealistic3DTileset`, the OSM imagery
provider and Ion world terrain are all Earth-only, so `src/maps/` would need a
second catalogue rather than a swapped token.

## The blast radius, measured

Setting `Ellipsoid.default` only moves the call sites that *don't* name an
ellipsoid. The ones that do are pinned to Earth forever:

| | count |
|---|---|
| explicit `Ellipsoid.WGS84` occurrences | **94** |
| non-test files containing them | **44** |
| hardcoded `6371` (mean Earth radius, km) | **21** |
| hardcoded `6378137` / `6356752` | 0 |

The concentration is in exactly the places you'd guess — `src/ui/cockpitCamera.js`
(7), `src/layers/launches/paths.js` (6), `src/cameraVerbs.js` (6),
`src/layers/launches/camera.js` (5), `src/data/motionModel.js` (5).

This is the part I'd flag hardest, because the failure mode is quiet: flip
`Ellipsoid.default` and the app *appears* to work while 94 call sites keep doing
Earth geometry. You get mixed-frame drift, not an exception. The 21 `6371`
constants are the same hazard — they live in ~16 private `haversineKm` /
`greatCircleKm` helpers scattered across the tree, each with its own copy.

Share-link state is tighter than it looks: `LAYER_STATE_REGISTRY` has **28 entries
with 28 single-character tokens**, and the charset is already
`12abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz` — it has spilled out of the alphabet into digits. A
world dimension needs a home in that grammar, and adding lunar/Mars layers pushes
on a namespace with no headroom left.

## The part that actually costs the most

**All 24 layer directories are Earth-*data* layers.** I classified them by their
real upstream hosts: NOAA NHC, USGS, NASA GIBS/CMR, InciWeb, OSM/DeFlock, city
bikeshare feeds, and so on. Not one of them means anything on another body.

So switching the globe doesn't make the app work on Mars — it makes it *wrong*. It
will cheerfully plot Texas traffic cameras on Mare Tranquillitatis, because nothing
in the app models which world a layer belongs to. I checked: there is no
world/celestial-body concept anywhere in `src/`.

Two specifics worth knowing:

- **`satellites` can't be reused, and it isn't a porting problem.** It's CelesTrak
  TLE + SGP4 (`src/layers/satellites/policy.js:5`). SGP4 is an Earth-orbit analytic
  propagator with Earth's gravity harmonics baked into the model — a Mars orbiter
  isn't a different input to it, it's outside its domain. Lunar and Mars orbiters
  need real ephemerides (SPICE kernels or JPL Horizons), which is a different
  propagation path, not a parameter.
- **The app already computes where the Moon is** —
  `celestialRing.js:628` uses `Simon1994PlanetaryPositions.computeMoonPositionInEarthInertialFrame`.
  That's the Moon as a *sky object seen from Earth*, which is the opposite of
  standing on it, but it means the astronomy dependency is already in the tree.

## A path that doesn't need a big-bang switch

Given it's not a near-term priority, the thing I'd argue for is an order where each
step is independently useful and independently revertible — so this can sit
half-done for a year without being a liability:

1. **World scope as metadata.** Add a `worlds` field to `LAYER_STATE_REGISTRY` (it
   already carries `id` / `token` / `disposition` / `optionOwner`) and have the
   shell hide layers that don't claim the current world. Default everything to
   `['earth']`. No globe switch, no camera work, no visible change — but it's the
   thing that makes every later step safe, and it's the piece that's missing.
2. **Make the ellipsoid injectable.** Replace the 94 explicit `Ellipsoid.WGS84`
   with a single accessor, and collapse the 21 `6371` into one shared helper. Pure
   refactor, behaviour-identical on Earth, and a count-based test can ratchet it to
   zero so it can't regress.
3. **One second globe — the Moon, not Mars.** Better data story, and the camera and
   terrain work is the same for both.
4. **Content layers.** Landing sites and rover traverses are small static datasets
   and fit the existing bundled-dataset contract in `src/data/local_data/` (source,
   upstream commit, licence, byte budget, tested).

Steps 1 and 2 are the ones I'd be happy to pick up, because they're measurable and
boring and they're what makes step 3 not a rewrite. Step 3 onward is a real
feature and should be somebody's deliberate decision, not a side effect.

## Data sources

For the record, so this doesn't get relitigated later: the usable public sources
are NASA/USGS Astrogeology controlled mosaics and DEMs, the NASA Trek WMTS services
(Moon Trek / Mars Trek), JPL Horizons for ephemerides, SPICE kernels for spacecraft
and rover frames, and the PDS archives for mission products. NASA-produced imagery
and data are generally free of copyright restriction with an attribution
convention rather than a licence, which fits `DATA_SOURCES.md` as-is — though I'd
want to pin exact endpoints and per-product terms before anyone writes a loader,
rather than trusting my summary here.

Happy to open step 1 as a small PR if you want to see the shape, or to leave this
as a note on the issue if you'd rather not carry the metadata until there's a
second world to use it. Either is fine — I'd rather ask than guess at the
direction.

Rebased onto `513dc87`. Green: **5,050 passing / 0 failing**, 13 allocation budgets,
plus `doctor` / `format:check` / `check:boundaries` / `build`.

Rebasing turned up something that makes this PR's case better than the one I
originally made for it, so it's worth saying plainly.

When I opened this, the argument was partly hypothetical — Radio owned the only
audio, so single-source playback was a property of there being one producer rather
than a guarantee anything enforced. #732 has since landed local FM demodulation,
and the tree now has **six** things that can make sound:

- `src/layers/radio/playback.js` (internet radio)
- `src/layers/radio/tuningNoise.js`
- `src/sdr/controller.js` (local FM, new)
- `src/voice/realtimeFacade.js`
- `src/voice/realtimeInput.js`
- `src/data/atcAudio.js` (only in #723, on top of this)

#732 already had to solve the collision, and solved it exactly the way you'd
expect for two producers — `localSdrControls.js` subscribes to both state streams
and stops the other side on takeover:

```js
_onReceiverState(state) {
  const fmAudioActive = localSdrFmAudioActive(state);
  // Local FM just started: it takes over from internet radio.
  if (fmAudioActive && !this._fmAudioActive) this._stopInternetRadio();
  ...
_onRadioState(state) {
  const radioAudioActive = internetRadioAudioActive(state);
  // Internet radio just started: it takes over from local FM.
  if (radioAudioActive && !this._radioAudioActive && this._fmAudioActive) { ... }
```

That's correct, and I'm not suggesting it should have been written differently at
the time. The point is only how it scales: pairwise takeover needs a directed check
per ordered pair, and the arbitration has to live somewhere that holds a reference
to every producer — here, a UI controller reaching across into two different
layers. A third producer turns two checks into six, and each new one has to be
taught about all the others.

The claim in this PR is the same guarantee at O(1) per producer: a producer says
"I'm taking the audio", gets told when it loses it, and never needs to know who
else exists. `src/sdr/controller.js` and `radio/playback.js` could adopt it
incrementally — one `claimAudio` call each — and `localSdrControls.js`'s
cross-layer wiring would then have nothing left to do.

I've deliberately **not** touched either of them in this PR. Retrofitting the two
existing producers is a separate change with its own risk, and it should be your
call whether it's wanted at all, not something I slip into a PR that's meant to add
one small module. Happy to do it as a follow-up if you want it.

Here's a summary of the changes in `server/providers/weather.js`:

1. **NOAA Pipeline (Zero Regressions):** All existing NOAA products (`radar`, `lightning`, `clouds`, `clouds-regional`) remain untouched. They still use `parseWeatherCapabilities()` for WMS XML parsing, `EPSG:4326` geographic bounding box math, and their original WMS `GetMap` workflow.
2. **Metadata Normalization (`/manifest`):** When `product === 'radar-global'`, the provider fetches RainViewer's `weather-maps.json`, converts timestamps to standard ISO 8601 strings, stores an in-memory `{ time -> framePath }` map, and returns a standard `schemaVersion: 1` manifest advertising `tilingScheme: 'web-mercator'`.
3. **Tile Resolution (`/tile`):**
   - **NOAA:** Continues building standard WMS `GetMap` URLs.
   - **RainViewer:** Routes `{z}/{x}/{y}` to RainViewer's WebMercator tile cache, clamping $z \le 7$ to allow Cesium client-side upscaling without 404s.
4. **Shared Infrastructure:** Both providers share in-flight request coalescing (`shared()`), the 16 MiB LRU tile cache, and the unified 13-frame timeline contract.

All 66 test suites in `weather.test.mjs` pass cleanly, confirming zero regressions on NOAA products.
